sf1.p1: What do music and technology have to do with one another? Quite a lot. After all, composers have often been fascinated by the latest technical inventions of their time.
sf1.p2: It all began with Ludwig van Beethoven, who was the first to use Johann Nepomuk Mälzel’s groundbreaking technical invention – the metronome – in his compositions.
sf1.p3: Or Arthur Honegger, who, as a keen ‘trainspotter’ – that is, a fan of steam locomotives – set the impressive sounds of a large American steam locomotive to music in 1923: you can almost hear it racing across the American continent at night…
sf1.p4: We move on to Niklosz Rosza, who, for the Theremin – introduced in 1920 – the first electric instrument to be played without physical contact – and it doesn’t stop there with the ‘Concerto for Smartphones and Orchestra’ by the French composer Bernard Cavanna.
sf1.p5: We performed this and other tech-inspired pieces of music with young people from Frankfurt (Oder) and Schwedt.
sf2.p1: **Johann Wolfgang von Goethe:** *He who knows himself and others / Will realise here too / That the East and the West / Can no longer be separated*
sf2.p2: **Rudyard Kipling:** *East is East, West is West, and never the twain shall meet*
sf2.p3: **Who is right? Goethe? Kipling? Both? Perhaps – a bit of both?**
sf2.p4: We explored this together with young people from Strausberg and Frankfurt (Oder) as part of this educational project – through music and drama.
sf2.p5: We have been looking at the Spannungsfeldern and the differences that can both divide and unite people.
sf2.p6: The unfamiliar can be frightening, and fear can lead to wars. Where does this militant rejection of the unknown come from?
sf2.p7: And yet, the strange and the unknown have time and again held people in their spell. Why, one might ask, have daring explorers throughout the ages sought to discover the world – or unknown worlds?
sf2.p8: Why does the foreign and unknown repel some people and frighten them? Why does the foreign and unknown magically attract others and spark their curiosity?
sf2.p9: Together with the young people, we used music and art to explore how the East and the West have been at war with one another for centuries, whilst at the same time observing, influencing and learning from one another with great curiosity for just as long.
sf2.p10: That is why the simple formula is not true: East is East and West is West. No, the West has long since arrived in the East, and the East has long since arrived in the West. So Goethe was right.
sf2.p11: Music is a wonderful language for describing these bridges and the ‘peaceful conquests’ of the East by the West, and of the West by the East. It has been for centuries. It needs no words; you just have to listen carefully. That is exactly what we have done with this project and what we have passed on.
sf2.credits: With Howard Griffiths as musical director and pupils from the Europa-Gymnasium Frankfurt (Oder) and the Strausberg Upper Secondary School.
sf3.p1: *“The man asked: ‘Who are you?’ – ‘I am Death, who makes everyone equal.’ Then the man said: ‘You are the right one; you take the rich and the poor alike, without distinction; you shall be my son’s godfather …*
sf3.p2: *… ‘You see,’ said Death, ‘those are the lights of people’s lives. The big ones belong to children, the medium-sized ones to married couples in their prime, and the small ones to the elderly. Yet even children and young people often have only a tiny little light.’*
sf3.source: From ‘Grim Reaper’, a fairy tale by the Brothers Grimm
sf3.p3: Is it fair that a child should die whilst an elderly person is allowed to live for a long time? Is it fair that someone who has money can buy good health, whilst someone who is poor has to die sooner? Is death, which is said to make everyone equal, really fair? Is there a difference between LAW and JUSTICE? Is it even worth giving these thoughts any consideration? Especially when you’re young?
sf3.p4: We believe the answer is yes. It is always worth reflecting on the finiteness of one’s life. Not just when life is drawing to a close – but also right here and now. To realise just how precious every day is.
sf3.p5: It is worth discussing the topic of justice. Is there such a thing as absolute justice? And where does it come from, or who provides it? And who adheres to it? Or does everyone have their own definition of justice?
sf3.p6: We explored these fascinating questions together with pupils from classes Frankfurt (Oder) and Słubice. This led to some very engaging discussions and a multimedia performance featuring music, dance, drama and shadow theatre.
sf3.credits: With Howard Griffiths as musical director and featuring pupils from the Freie Waldorfschule Frankfurt and the Słubicer Uniwersyteckie Liceum Ogólnokształcące.
sf4.p1: We live in times when the most powerful politicians blatantly distort the truth and label lies as ‘alternative facts’, when inconvenient facts are redefined as ‘fake news’ on social media, and when it is becoming increasingly difficult to distinguish between lies and the truth. It would be nice if there were an absolute truth to hold on to.
sf4.p2: Rock star Jimi Hendrix claimed to have found this truth in music and said: “Music doesn’t lie.” Whether he was right about that … we explored this with pupils from Frankfurt’s Karl-Liebknecht-Gymnasium and the Lyzeum Słubice, using music by Shostakovich, Massenet, Mozart and others.
sf4.p3: This educational project also saw the world premiere of another work by the young English composer Alexander Papp.
sf5.p1: Fear is something you need to get out of the habit of feeling. Nobody needs fear. Being fearless and brave – that’s what counts. That’s right, isn’t it? Life says: wrong. Life says that courage and fear go hand in hand.
sf5.p2: Fear is the warning light in our heads. It flashes red when something is wrong, when danger looms, when we become too careless, or when we take too great a risk. But when fear becomes too overwhelming, when it tries to take control and we let it dictate our actions – then there’s only one thing that helps: courage.
sf5.p3: We need courage to venture out of our comfort zone, to defend our opinions, our ideals and our freedom. Courage ensures that we are not helplessly at the mercy of our fears.
sf5.p4: In this educational project with German and Polish young people, we want to explore how courage and fear are intertwined, how fear lurks everywhere, how not to let it paralyse us, and how courage can be trained just like a muscle – and bring these ideas to life on stage in a multimedia production: through choreography, mime, drawing, film and rhetoric.
sf5.p5: Texts written by the pupils taking part on the themes of courage and fear will be read out.
sf5.credits: Howard Griffiths is the musical director.
